name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

**Minimal equivalent rewrites** are allowed when Verus genuinely cannot express
a construct. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory. Check `std_specs/`, recent additions.
3. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — rewrite the smallest possible expression
   to an equivalent one Verus accepts. Requirements:
   - Same semantics (identical observable behavior for all inputs)
   - Same panic/error behavior
   - Same asymptotic time and space complexity
   - Smallest possible diff
   - `// VERUS REWRITE: <reason>` comment on the changed code
   - Minimal reproducer proving the original is unsupported
4. **Stdlib wrapper** — if a stdlib/core function call fails because Verus
   cannot handle the parameter types (e.g., `&mut [T]` from `DerefMut`
   coercion, closures), create a thin wrapper function whose body contains
   **ONLY** the stdlib call. Mark the wrapper `external_body` with pre/post
   conditions. The original function calls the wrapper instead. This isolates
   the trust boundary to the thinnest possible layer.

   Example — `core::mem::replace` on `&mut Vec<T>[index]`:
   ```rust
   #[verus_verify(external_body)]
   #[verus_spec(prev =>
       requires index < old(v)@.len(),
       ensures
           prev == old(v)@[index as int],
           v@ == old(v)@.update(index as int, value),
           v@.len() == old(v)@.len(),
   )]
   fn vec_replace<T>(v: &mut Vec<T>, index: usize, value: T) -> T {
       ::core::mem::replace(&mut v[index], value)
   }
   ```
   The wrapper body is a single stdlib call. The `external_body` trusts only
   this one line. The calling function remains fully body-verified.

5. **`external_body` on the original** — absolute last resort. Requires a
   minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry.

**Principle:** prefer rewriting code to a semantic equivalent over ANY cheating.
A rewrite that lets Verus verify the body is always better than `external_body`.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition.
- **Constants**: if the initializer uses only literals and Verus-visible
  symbols, Verus sees it directly — no duplication needed. If it references
  external symbols Verus cannot resolve (e.g. `mem::PAGE_SIZE`), add a
  spec duplicate inside `verus! {}` under `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]` with
  the literal value — but keep the original **ungated** so exec code still
  uses it. Never `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented
in `trust.md`.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in specification phase (must be eliminated in proving) |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Last resort — requires exhausting the escalation ladder (verify as-is → vstd search → minimal rewrite → stdlib wrapper). Must have minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |

## trust.md

Any use of the following MUST be documented in `trust.md` (in the logs directory):
- `external_body` on any function
- `admit()` remaining after proving phase
- `assume(...)` anywhere
- `cfg-gated exec code` (beyond imports/derives/logging)
- `assume_specification` or `axiom`

Each entry must include:
1. Function name and file:line location
2. What trust item was used
3. Minimal reproducer proving it cannot be avoided
4. Classification: `STDLIB_WRAPPER` / `VERUS_LIMITATION` / `EXTERNAL_TYPE` / `TEMPORARY`

`trust.md` is an **audit log**, not approval. Items classified `TEMPORARY`
are blockers that must be resolved. Items with no reproducer are blockers.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

**`axiom` requires human approval** — it introduces arbitrary unverified
axioms with no connection to an external API contract.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
the actual vstd source thoroughly:

```bash
grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
```

Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
`vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## Claiming Verus Limitations

**Principle: isolate and test before concluding.** A failing expression is
evidence only about that expression — not about broader language features —
until a smaller isolated reproducer shows the specific construct also fails.

When `f(|x| expr)` fails, the error might be in `f`, in `|x|`, in `expr`,
or in the combination. You **cannot** conclude "closures are unsupported"
from one failed call. You must test each component separately.

**Do not generalize from an unsupported API to a feature class.** If
`v.sort_by_key(|x| x.field)` fails, that is evidence about `sort_by_key` (or
about `&mut` complex args), not about closures. You must isolate and test
the closure by itself before claiming closures are unsupported.

### Required diagnostic steps

Before claiming any construct is unsupported, you **must**:

1. **Read the actual error.** Verus errors are specific — "partition_point is
   not supported" means `partition_point` lacks a spec, not that closures fail.
2. **Isolate the construct.** Write a minimal standalone `.rs` file that tests
   ONLY the construct you suspect is unsupported. **Run it through Verus** and
   quote the actual error. Do not claim "X is unsupported" unless an isolated
   repro for X itself fails.
   - If a closure-taking function fails, test a standalone closure first,
     then test a simpler closure-taking API (e.g., `Option::map`).
   - If a for-loop over an iterator fails, test `for x in vec` first.
3. **Search for counterexamples** in `verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`
   and in vstd source. If others use the construct successfully, your problem
   is elsewhere.
4. **Search vstd** — `grep -r` across the entire vstd directory. Check
   `std_specs/` for `assume_specification` on stdlib functions.
5. **Apply an approved workaround** if one matches:
   - `|_|` → `|_e|` (Verus requires named variables in closures)
   - Incompatible derives → `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]`
   - `debug_assert!` / logging macros → `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on the statement
6. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — follow the escalation ladder in Source
   Integrity. Only after isolated repro confirms the specific construct fails.
7. **Stdlib wrapper** — only after isolated repro shows the API call itself
   is the failing unit (see Source Integrity step 4).

### Examples of past false generalizations

| Error on | False conclusion | Reality |
|---|---|---|
| `v.partition_point(\|x\| ...)` | "closures not supported" | `partition_point` lacks vstd spec; closures work fine |
| `v.sort_by_key(\|x\| ...)` | "closures not supported" | `&mut` complex args unsupported; closures work fine |
| `for x in v.windows(2)` | "iterators not supported" | `Windows` lacks `ForLoopGhostIteratorNew`; `for x in vec` works |
| `for i in (0..n).rev()` | "ranges not supported" | `Rev<Range>` lacks trait impl; `for i in 0..n` works |
| `x.ok_or_else(\|\| err)` | "closures not supported" | Works — vstd has `assume_specification` for it |

### Guardrails

description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

**Minimal equivalent rewrites** are allowed when Verus genuinely cannot express
a construct. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory. Check `std_specs/`, recent additions.
3. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — rewrite the smallest possible expression
   to an equivalent one Verus accepts. Requirements:
   - Same semantics (identical observable behavior for all inputs)
   - Same panic/error behavior
   - Same asymptotic time and space complexity
   - Smallest possible diff
   - `// VERUS REWRITE: <reason>` comment on the changed code
   - Minimal reproducer proving the original is unsupported
4. **Stdlib wrapper** — if a stdlib/core function call fails because Verus
   cannot handle the parameter types (e.g., `&mut [T]` from `DerefMut`
   coercion, closures), create a thin wrapper function whose body contains
   **ONLY** the stdlib call. Mark the wrapper `external_body` with pre/post
   conditions. The original function calls the wrapper instead. This isolates
   the trust boundary to the thinnest possible layer.

   Example — `core::mem::replace` on `&mut Vec<T>[index]`:
   ```rust
   #[verus_verify(external_body)]
   #[verus_spec(prev =>
       requires index < old(v)@.len(),
       ensures
           prev == old(v)@[index as int],
           v@ == old(v)@.update(index as int, value),
           v@.len() == old(v)@.len(),
   )]
   fn vec_replace<T>(v: &mut Vec<T>, index: usize, value: T) -> T {
       ::core::mem::replace(&mut v[index], value)
   }
   ```
   The wrapper body is a single stdlib call. The `external_body` trusts only
   this one line. The calling function remains fully body-verified.

5. **`external_body` on the original** — absolute last resort. Requires a
   minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry.

**Principle:** prefer rewriting code to a semantic equivalent over ANY cheating.
A rewrite that lets Verus verify the body is always better than `external_body`.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition.
- **Constants**: if the initializer uses only literals and Verus-visible
  symbols, Verus sees it directly — no duplication needed. If it references
  external symbols Verus cannot resolve (e.g. `mem::PAGE_SIZE`), add a
  spec duplicate inside `verus! {}` under `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]` with
  the literal value — but keep the original **ungated** so exec code still
  uses it. Never `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),

used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),

state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),

source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented
in `trust.md`.

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in specification phase (must be eliminated in proving) |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | Last resort — requires exhausting the escalation ladder (verify as-is → vstd search → minimal rewrite → stdlib wrapper). Must have minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |

## trust.md

Any use of the following MUST be documented in `trust.md` (in the logs directory):
- `external_body` on any function
- `admit()` remaining after proving phase
- `assume(...)` anywhere
- `cfg-gated exec code` (beyond imports/derives/logging)
- `assume_specification` or `axiom`

Each entry must include:
1. Function name and file:line location
2. What trust item was used
3. Minimal reproducer proving it cannot be avoided
4. Classification: `STDLIB_WRAPPER` / `VERUS_LIMITATION` / `EXTERNAL_TYPE` / `TEMPORARY`

`trust.md` is an **audit log**, not approval. Items classified `TEMPORARY`
are blockers that must be resolved. Items with no reproducer are blockers.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

**`axiom` requires human approval** — it introduces arbitrary unverified
axioms with no connection to an external API contract.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
the actual vstd source thoroughly:

```bash
grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
```

Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
`vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

**Principle: isolate and test before concluding.** A failing expression is
evidence only about that expression — not about broader language features —
until a smaller isolated reproducer shows the specific construct also fails.

When `f(|x| expr)` fails, the error might be in `f`, in `|x|`, in `expr`,
or in the combination. You **cannot** conclude "closures are unsupported"
from one failed call. You must test each component separately.

**Do not generalize from an unsupported API to a feature class.** If

the closure by itself before claiming closures are unsupported.

1. **Read the actual error.** Verus errors are specific — "partition_point is
   not supported" means `partition_point` lacks a spec, not that closures fail.
2. **Isolate the construct.** Write a minimal standalone `.rs` file that tests
   ONLY the construct you suspect is unsupported. **Run it through Verus** and
   quote the actual error. Do not claim "X is unsupported" unless an isolated
   repro for X itself fails.

     then test a simpler closure-taking API (e.g., `Option::map`).
   - If a for-loop over an iterator fails, test `for x in vec` first.
3. **Search for counterexamples** in `verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`
   and in vstd source. If others use the construct successfully, your problem
   is elsewhere.
4. **Search vstd** — `grep -r` across the entire vstd directory. Check
   `std_specs/` for `assume_specification` on stdlib functions.
5. **Apply an approved workaround** if one matches:
   - `|_|` → `|_e|` (Verus requires named variables in closures)
   - Incompatible derives → `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]`
   - `debug_assert!` / logging macros → `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on the statement

   Integrity. Only after isolated repro confirms the specific construct fails.

name: ast-consistency
description: "AST-level exec fidelity checking tools and pre-approved deviations. Use after modifying source files to verify exec code is unchanged."
---

# AST Consistency Check

Source exec code must not change during verification — see `verus-constraints`
for the full rules. This skill covers the **tooling** to enforce that guarantee.

## Tools

The checker uses tree-sitter to hash exec code after stripping all
ghost/proof/spec annotations. It detects changes invisible to textual diff.

`scripts/ast_consistency.py` provides four subcommands:
- `count` — quick pass/fail
- `summary` — per-element status table
- `diff --name "Fn::name"` — unified diff for one function/struct
- `report -o <dir>` — full report with all diffs

The `source` argument is optional. Use `--base-ref` to extract the original
from git, or omit both on `verus-ai/*` branches for auto-detection:

```bash
# Explicit original file:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py original.rs verified.rs count

# Via git ref:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py --base-ref main verified.rs count

# Auto-detect on verus-ai/* branches:
python3 scripts/ast_consistency.py verified.rs count
```

`diff` with `--full` shows specs; default is exec-only.

**MCP alternative**: If the `verus-ast` MCP server is registered, the same
functionality is available as tools (`ast_count`, `ast_summary`, `ast_diff`,
`ast_report`) with the same auto-detection.

## Pre-Approved Deviations

These minimal exec changes are known Verus limitations — no full deviation
process needed, but still document with a comment:

| Original | Verus Version | Reason |
|----------|--------------|--------|
| `self.x += 1` | `self.x = self.x + 1` | Compound assignment unsupported |
| `self.arr[i] \|= v` | `self.arr.set(i, self.arr[i] \| v)` | Mutable index unsupported |
| `-> T` | `-> (ret: T)` | Named returns for ensures |
| `#[derive(Clone, ...)]` | `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))] #[derive(...)]` | cfg-gating incompatible derives |
| `Ok(Self { .. })` | `let result = Self { .. }; Ok(result)` | Ensures needs to reference return value |
| `f(complex_expr)` | `let x = complex_expr; f(x)` | Intermediate value for assertions |
| `.ok_or_else(\|\| ...)` | `match ... { Some(v) => v, None => return Err(...) }` | Closures unsupported in some contexts |

## Handling MISMATCHes

When the checker reports a MISMATCH:

1. **Default: restore original code.** Exec changes are violations. Use
   `git show <base_ref>:path/to/file.rs` to view the original, then
   manually restore the changed exec code while keeping your annotations.
   Adapt the proof to the original code — not the other way around.
2. **Check pre-approved deviations.** If the change matches one above,
   keep it but add a comment documenting which deviation and why.
3. **Verify it's a real Verus limitation.** Before accepting any other
   change, confirm Verus genuinely cannot handle the original construct:
   - Search vstd for existing support (e.g. `checked_mul` has vstd specs)
   - Try alternative proof strategies that preserve the original code
   - Build a minimal reproducer proving the limitation
4. **If confirmed, document with full justification.** Add a `VERUS DEVIATION`
   comment explaining: what was changed, why the original doesn't work,
   what alternatives were tried, and why this is the smallest possible change.

# Verus Verification Review Methodology

Review verification code with the same rigor as the verification itself. A
rubber-stamp review is worse than no review — it gives false confidence.

## Core Principles

- **Implementation is ground truth.** Check every spec against actual code
  behavior, not against what you think the code should do.
- **Stay independent and skeptical.** Do not trust claims at face value —
  not fix reports, not "it's a Verus limitation", not "the spec has to be
  that way". Verify everything yourself: read the code, run the commands,
  search vstd, reproduce the claimed limitation. Form your own judgment.
- **Be specific and actionable.** Every issue must point to a specific
  location and describe a specific fix. "Specs could be stronger" is not
  actionable. "`insert` is missing ensures for error code when table is full" is.

## Review Focus

### Primary: Spec Quality (reviewer's unique value)

If verification passes, the proof is correct — don't review proof technique.
Focus on whether specs are **meaningful and complete**. Refer to `spec-design`
skill for what good specs look like.

The reviewer's core mental model: **read each ensures clause as a caller who
has never seen the implementation.** Is every clause natural, directly usable,
and free of implementation assumptions? If you find yourself needing to look
at the code to understand why a clause is phrased that way, the spec is
probably mirroring the implementation.

- **Requires**: are preconditions necessary? Would the function work without
  them? Unnecessary requires narrow the usable interface.
- **Ensures**: are postconditions strong enough? Do they capture what callers
  actually need? `Err(_) => true` is useless.
- **Loop invariants**: do they capture the full state at each iteration, or
  do they only state what the prover needs to terminate?
- **Completeness**: are error paths specified? Is state preservation on error
  proven? Are there bidirectional failure conditions ("fails IFF X")?
- **Liveness**: under what conditions does the operation succeed?
  (`can_do_X() ==> result is Ok`)
- **Abstraction**: does the View type hide implementation details? Could the
  implementation be replaced without changing the View?

When reviewing a proposed fix, apply the same caller mental model: did the
fix express the missing property at the right abstraction level, or did it
patch the existing spec using implementation knowledge?

### Automated Checks (verify, don't review)

These should be confirmed but don't require judgment. See `proving-guide`
for verification tools and `ast-consistency` for exec fidelity tools.
- **Verification passes**: `make verify` reports 0 errors
- **Guardrails compliance**: no admit, assume, external_body, trusted,
  cfg-gated exec code (use `detect_cheating` tool or `verus-constraints` rules)
- **Compilation**: `cargo build` succeeds without Verus features
- **Exec fidelity**: `ast-consistency` tools show no unintended changes

If you spot potential bugs during review, refer to `bug-reporting` skill for
classification and reporting format.

## Adversarial Dialogue (post-review)

When the pipeline enters dialogue mode after bulk fixes fail, the reviewer
drives a focused, turn-by-turn conversation with the fixer. Each turn
targets one specific issue (or a tightly-coupled bundle sharing one root cause).

### Skeptical Verifier Mindset

- **Don't trust claims.** If the fixer says "this is a Verus limitation" or
  "this can't be expressed", verify it yourself. Run the tool, read the error,
  search for counterexamples.
- **Search for precedent.** Before accepting a limitation claim, search known
  Verus projects (`verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`,
  ironfleet, page-table examples) for similar patterns that work.
- **Ask "why".** Demand specific evidence: error messages, minimal
  reproduction, links to Verus issues. "It doesn't work" is not evidence.
- **Don't be lazy.** Always use tools — run `make verify`, read files, search
  code. Never accept or reject a claim without checking it yourself.
- **Know when to stop.** A genuine limitation has: (a) a specific Verus error
  message, (b) no known workaround in verus-lang examples, (c) a clear
  explanation of why the pattern is unsupported. Mark such items BLOCKED
  with the evidence attached.

### Dialogue Protocol

Each reviewer turn writes a focused request file. To end the dialogue,
create the designated STOP file with content `RESOLVED` or `BLOCKED`.
Do not create the STOP file while issues remain unaddressed.

15. // BTreeMap is from alloc::collections. vstd provides specs in vstd::std_specs::btree,

18. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(K)]
19. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
20. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(A)]
21. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
22. #[verifier::external_body]
23. pub struct ExBTreeMap<K, V, A>(alloc::collections::BTreeMap<K, V, A>)
24.     where A: core::alloc::Allocator + core::clone::Clone;
25. 
26. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
27. pub struct ExGlobal(alloc::alloc::Global);
28. 
29. // CacheEntry is a private internal type.
30. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
31. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
32. struct ExCacheEntry<V>(crate::CacheEntry<V>);
33. 
34. // CacheGuard wraps &mut V; Verus cannot handle &mut in struct fields,
35. // so we declare it as an external type.
36. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
37. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
38. #[verifier::external_body]
39. pub struct ExCacheGuard<'a, V>(crate::CacheGuard<'a, V>);
40. 
41. //==================================================================================================
42. // CacheView - Abstract Specification Model
43. //==================================================================================================
44. 
45. /// Abstract view of a bounded LRU cache.
46. ///
47. /// - `contents`: the key-value mapping of all cached entries.
48. /// - `capacity`: maximum number of entries.
49. /// - `lru_order`: keys ordered from LRU (index 0) to MRU (last element).
50. #[verifier::ext_equal]
51. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(K)]
52. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
53. pub struct CacheView<K, V> {
54.     pub contents: Map<K, V>,
55.     pub capacity: nat,
56.     pub lru_order: Seq<K>,
57. }
58. 
59. impl<K, V> CacheView<K, V> {
60. 
61.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
62.     // Well-formedness Invariant
63.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
64. 
65.     /// Well-formedness invariant for the abstract cache state.
66.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
67.         // Size never exceeds capacity.
68.         &&& self.contents.dom().len() <= self.capacity
69.         // LRU order has no duplicates.
70.         &&& self.lru_order.no_duplicates()
71.         // LRU order contains exactly the stored keys.
72.         &&& self.lru_order.to_set() == self.contents.dom()
73.         // Explicit cardinality link (helps the solver).
74.         &&& self.lru_order.len() == self.contents.dom().len()
75.     }
76. 
77.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
78.     // Helper Spec Functions
79.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
80. 
81.     /// Move `key` to the most-recently-used position (end of the sequence).
82.     /// Preserves all other elements and their relative order.
83.     pub open spec fn move_to_mru(self, key: K) -> Seq<K> {
84.         self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key).push(key)
85.     }
86. 
87.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
88.     // Spec Transition Functions
89.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
90. 
91.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::new`.
92.     pub open spec fn spec_new(capacity: nat) -> CacheView<K, V> {
93.         CacheView {
94.             contents: Map::empty(),
95.             capacity,
96.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
97.         }
98.     }
99. 
100.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::get`.
101.     /// Returns the updated cache state and the lookup result.
102.     pub open spec fn spec_get(self, key: K) -> (CacheView<K, V>, Option<V>) {
103.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
104.             (CacheView {
105.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
106.                 ..self
107.             }, Some(self.contents[key]))
108.         } else {
109.             (self, None)
110.         }
111.     }
112. 
113.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::put`.
114.     pub open spec fn spec_put(self, key: K, value: V) -> CacheView<K, V> {
115.         if self.capacity == 0 {
116.             // Zero-capacity cache: no-op.
117.             self
118.         } else if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
119.             // Overwrite existing key: replace value, refresh recency.
120.             CacheView {
121.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
122.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
123.                 ..self
124.             }
125.         } else if self.contents.dom().len() >= self.capacity {
126.             // At capacity with new key: evict LRU victim, then insert.
127.             let victim = self.lru_order[0];
128.             CacheView {
129.                 contents: self.contents.remove(victim).insert(key, value),
130.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.subrange(1, self.lru_order.len() as int).push(key),
131.                 ..self
132.             }
133.         } else {
134.             // Below capacity with new key: insert directly.
135.             CacheView {
136.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
137.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.push(key),
138.                 ..self
139.             }
140.         }
141.     }
142. 
143.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::remove`.
144.     pub open spec fn spec_remove(self, key: K) -> CacheView<K, V> {
145.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
146.             CacheView {
147.                 contents: self.contents.remove(key),
148.                 lru_order: self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key),
149.                 ..self
150.             }
151.         } else {
152.             // Key absent: no-op.
153.             self
154.         }
155.     }
156. 
157.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::clear`.
158.     pub open spec fn spec_clear(self) -> CacheView<K, V> {
159.         CacheView {
160.             contents: Map::empty(),
161.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
162.             ..self  // capacity preserved
163.         }
164.     }
165. }

# Verus Verification Review Methodology

Review verification code with the same rigor as the verification itself. A
rubber-stamp review is worse than no review — it gives false confidence.

## Core Principles

- **Implementation is ground truth.** Check every spec against actual code
  behavior, not against what you think the code should do.
- **Stay independent and skeptical.** Do not trust claims at face value —
  not fix reports, not "it's a Verus limitation", not "the spec has to be
  that way". Verify everything yourself: read the code, run the commands,
  search vstd, reproduce the claimed limitation. Form your own judgment.
- **Be specific and actionable.** Every issue must point to a specific
  location and describe a specific fix. "Specs could be stronger" is not
  actionable. "`insert` is missing ensures for error code when table is full" is.

## Review Focus

### Primary: Spec Quality (reviewer's unique value)

If verification passes, the proof is correct — don't review proof technique.
Focus on whether specs are **meaningful and complete**. Refer to `spec-design`
skill for what good specs look like.

The reviewer's core mental model: **read each ensures clause as a caller who
has never seen the implementation.** Is every clause natural, directly usable,
and free of implementation assumptions? If you find yourself needing to look
at the code to understand why a clause is phrased that way, the spec is
probably mirroring the implementation.

- **Requires**: are preconditions necessary? Would the function work without
  them? Unnecessary requires narrow the usable interface.
- **Ensures**: are postconditions strong enough? Do they capture what callers
  actually need? `Err(_) => true` is useless.
- **Loop invariants**: do they capture the full state at each iteration, or
  do they only state what the prover needs to terminate?
- **Completeness**: are error paths specified? Is state preservation on error
  proven? Are there bidirectional failure conditions ("fails IFF X")?
- **Liveness**: under what conditions does the operation succeed?
  (`can_do_X() ==> result is Ok`)
- **Abstraction**: does the View type hide implementation details? Could the
  implementation be replaced without changing the View?

When reviewing a proposed fix, apply the same caller mental model: did the
fix express the missing property at the right abstraction level, or did it
patch the existing spec using implementation knowledge?

### Automated Checks (verify, don't review)

These should be confirmed but don't require judgment. See `proving-guide`
for verification tools and `ast-consistency` for exec fidelity tools.
- **Verification passes**: `make verify` reports 0 errors
- **Guardrails compliance**: no admit, assume, external_body, trusted,
  cfg-gated exec code (use `detect_cheating` tool or `verus-constraints` rules)
- **Compilation**: `cargo build` succeeds without Verus features
- **Exec fidelity**: `ast-consistency` tools show no unintended changes

If you spot potential bugs during review, refer to `bug-reporting` skill for
classification and reporting format.

## Adversarial Dialogue (post-review)

When the pipeline enters dialogue mode after bulk fixes fail, the reviewer
drives a focused, turn-by-turn conversation with the fixer. Each turn
targets one specific issue (or a tightly-coupled bundle sharing one root cause).

### Skeptical Verifier Mindset

- **Don't trust claims.** If the fixer says "this is a Verus limitation" or
  "this can't be expressed", verify it yourself. Run the tool, read the error,
  search for counterexamples.
- **Search for precedent.** Before accepting a limitation claim, search known
  Verus projects (`verus-lang/verus/source/rust_verify_test/tests/`,
  ironfleet, page-table examples) for similar patterns that work.
- **Ask "why".** Demand specific evidence: error messages, minimal
  reproduction, links to Verus issues. "It doesn't work" is not evidence.
- **Don't be lazy.** Always use tools — run `make verify`, read files, search
  code. Never accept or reject a claim without checking it yourself.
- **Know when to stop.** A genuine limitation has: (a) a specific Verus error
  message, (b) no known workaround in verus-lang examples, (c) a clear
  explanation of why the pattern is unsupported. Mark such items BLOCKED
  with the evidence attached.

### Dialogue Protocol

Each reviewer turn writes a focused request file. To end the dialogue,
create the designated STOP file with content `RESOLVED` or `BLOCKED`.
Do not create the STOP file while issues remain unaddressed.

125.         }
126.     } else if self.contents.dom().len() >= self.capacity {

128.         let victim = self.lru_order[0];
129.         CacheView {

131.             lru_order: self.lru_order.subrange(1, self.lru_order.len() as int).push(key),
132.             ..self
133.         }
134.     } else {
135.         // Below capacity with new key: insert directly.
136.         CacheView {
137.             contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
138.             lru_order: self.lru_order.push(key),
139.             ..self
140.         }

145. - **Eviction safety:** the branch `contents.dom().len() >= capacity` with

152. pub open spec fn spec_remove(self, key: K) -> CacheView<K, V> {
153.     if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
154.         CacheView {
155.             contents: self.contents.remove(key),
156.             lru_order: self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key),
157.             ..self
158.         }
159.     } else {

161.         self

169. pub open spec fn spec_clear(self) -> CacheView<K, V> {

171.         contents: Map::empty(),
172.         lru_order: Seq::empty(),

180. ## CacheGuard Modeling
181. 
182. `CacheGuard<'_, V>` implements `Deref<Target=V>` and `DerefMut`.  It is a
183. transparent borrow wrapper over `&mut V` — the value stored inside the cache.
184. 
185. **Design decision: no separate GuardView type.**
186. 
187. Rationale:
188. 
189. 1. **The guard is a thin smart pointer.**  Its only abstract state is the value
190.    it dereferences to.  A `GuardView<V>` would contain a single field `value: V`
191.    — isomorphic to `V` itself, adding no information.
192. 
193. 2. **Verus handles `&mut` natively.**  When `get(&mut self)` returns a
194.    `CacheGuard<'_, V>`, Verus tracks the mutable borrow.  While the guard is
195.    live the cache is exclusively borrowed; when the guard is dropped, any
196.    mutations to `*guard` are reflected in the cache's post-state.  This is
197.    standard `&mut` semantics, not a cache-specific concern.
198. 
199. 3. **Spec-phase guidance:**
200.    - The `get` ensures clause will state `*result == old(self)@.contents[key]`

200.    - The `get` ensures clause will state `*result == old(self)@.contents[key]`
201.      (value identity on return).
202.    - The recency update (`move_to_mru`) is captured in `self@` vs `old(self)@`.
203.    - Value mutations through the guard modify only `contents[key]`; `lru_order`
204.      and `capacity` are unaffected.
205. 
206. ---

208. ## Design Rationale
209. 
210. ### Field: `contents: Map<K, V>`
211. 
212. - **What it represents:** the set of key-value pairs currently stored.
213. - **Substitution test:** ✅ — any cache implementation, regardless of backing
214.   data structure (hash map, B-tree, array, linked list), maintains a logical
215.   key-value mapping.
216. - **Used in:** every spec transition (get, put, remove, clear) and `inv()`.
217. 
218. ### Field: `capacity: nat`
219. 
220. - **What it represents:** the upper bound on the number of entries.
221. - **Substitution test:** ✅ — any bounded cache has a configurable capacity.
222.   Using `nat` (not `usize`) avoids unnecessary overflow reasoning in specs.
223. - **Used in:** `inv()` (capacity bound) and `spec_put` (eviction decision).
224. 
225. ### Field: `lru_order: Seq<K>`
226. 
227. - **What it represents:** the recency ordering of all cached keys, from
228.   least-recently-used (index 0) to most-recently-used (last element).
229. - **Substitution test:** ✅ — any LRU cache must maintain a total recency
230.   order over its entries, regardless of whether the implementation uses
231.   counters, linked lists, timestamps, or something else.  The ordering is
232.   directly observable through eviction behavior: callers can determine which
233.   entry will be evicted next.

248.   counter, violating the substitution test.

260.   creates a consistency obligation (`size == contents.dom().len()`) in every

277.

280.   LRU victim changes.  Tracking only the current victim doesn't let us reason
281.   about how sequences of operations affect eviction order.  The full ordering
282.   is needed for compositional reasoning.

288.   state is just the value itself — a `GuardView` would be isomorphic to `V` and
289.   add no information.  Verus handles `&mut` borrows natively; the cache's

15.     /// The key-value mapping of all cached entries.
16.     pub contents: Map<K, V>,
17.     /// Maximum number of entries the cache can hold.
18.     pub capacity: nat,

20.     pub lru_order: Seq<K>,
21. }

25.

27. caller-visible state, using `Map`, `Seq`, and `nat` instead of machine types.
28.

34. impl<K, V> CacheView<K, V> {
35.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
36.         // 1. Size never exceeds the configured capacity.
37.         &&& self.contents.dom().len() <= self.capacity
38.         // 2. LRU order contains exactly the stored keys, without duplicates.
39.         &&& self.lru_order.no_duplicates()
40.         &&& self.lru_order.to_set() == self.contents.dom()
41.         // 3. Explicit cardinality link (derivable from 2, but helps the solver).
42.         &&& self.lru_order.len() == self.contents.dom().len()
43.     }
44. }

48. 
49. | # | Clause | Purpose |

4. //! Bounded LRU cache backed by `BTreeMap`.
5. //!
6. //! Entries are stored in a `BTreeMap` keyed by a caller-chosen type `K` that
7. //! implements `Ord + Clone`. A monotonic counter tracks access order; on
8. //! eviction the entry with the smallest (oldest) counter value is removed.
9. //! Lookups bump the counter to mark the entry as recently used.
10. //!
11. //! # Capacity
12. //!
13. //! The cache is bounded by a capacity given at construction time. When the
14. //! cache is full, the least-recently-used entry is evicted before inserting a
15. //! new one.
16. //!
17. //! # Example
18. //!
19. //! ```
20. //! use cache::Cache;
21. //!
22. //! let mut cache: Cache<&str, i32> = Cache::new(2);
23. //! cache.put("a", 1);

26. //!
27. //! // Inserting a third entry evicts "b" (least recently used).
28. //! cache.put("c", 3);

3. ## BUG-1: Counter overflow (u64)
4. 
5. - **Status:** UNCONFIRMED
6. - **Severity:** LOW (physically unreachable)
7. - **Location:** `lib.rs` — `Cache::get` (line ~192) and `Cache::put` (line ~224)
8. - **Description:** The `counter: u64` field is incremented on every `get` hit and
9.   `put` call without overflow checking (`self.counter += 1`). After 2^64
10.   operations the counter wraps to 0, which would corrupt LRU ordering —
11.   freshly accessed entries would have a lower counter than old ones, causing
12.   incorrect eviction.
13. - **Impact:** At 10 billion ops/sec, overflow requires ~58 years of continuous
14.   operation. Physically unreachable in practice, but the spec does not model
15.   this assumption.
16. - **Spec gap:** No `requires self.counter < u64::MAX` precondition exists.
17.   The spec transition functions use abstract `Seq` ordering (not counters),
18.   so the spec is correct even if the implementation overflows — but the
19.   `external_body` trust gap means the implementation's correctness depends
20.   on no overflow occurring.
21. - **Recommendation:** Document as a trust assumption. Optionally add
22.   `debug_assert!(self.counter < u64::MAX)` or use `checked_add`.
23.

     ==> entries[k1].last_used != entries[k2].last_used
 ```
 
 **Applies to:** internal invariant, maintained by `new`, `get`, `put`, `clear`
 
 **Why needed:** Injectivity ensures that `min_by_key(last_used)` in `evict` produces a unique victim — the LRU entry is deterministic. Without this, the spec-level `lru_order[0]` might not correspond to the implementation's eviction choice. Also prevents non-deterministic tie-breaking in `min_by_key`.
 
 ---
 
 ### TYPE-5: LRU Order Matches Counter Order
 
 **Statement:** The `lru_order` sequence in the view is consistent with the `last_used` counter ordering: for any two entries at positions `i < j` in `lru_order`, the entry at position `i` has a strictly smaller `last_used` value than the entry at position `j`.
 
 **Applies to:** internal invariant linking concrete counters to abstract ordering
 
 **Formal sketch:**
 ```
 forall |i: int, j: int|
     0 <= i < j < self@.lru_order.len()
     ==> entries[lru_order[i]].last_used < entries[lru_order[j]].last_used
 ```
 
 **Why needed:** This is the key linking invariant that connects the counter-based implementation to the sequence-based abstract specification. It ensures that the min-by-key eviction in the implementation corresponds to removing `lru_order[0]` in the spec.

4. // Cache - Specifications
5. //
6. // This file contains the CacheView type, invariant, spec transition functions,

8. 
9. verus! {
10. 
11. //==================================================================================================
12. // External Type Specifications
13. //==================================================================================================
14. 
15. // BTreeMap is from alloc::collections. vstd provides specs in vstd::std_specs::btree,
16. // but they require cfg(std) which is incompatible with this crate's no_std kernel target.
17. // We declare it as an external type so Verus can reference it.
18. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(K)]
19. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
20. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(A)]
21. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
22. #[verifier::external_body]
23. pub struct ExBTreeMap<K, V, A>(alloc::collections::BTreeMap<K, V, A>)
24.     where A: core::alloc::Allocator + core::clone::Clone;
25. 
26. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
27. pub struct ExGlobal(alloc::alloc::Global);
28. 
29. // CacheEntry is a private internal type.
30. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
31. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
32. struct ExCacheEntry<V>(crate::CacheEntry<V>);
33. 
34. // CacheGuard wraps &mut V; Verus cannot handle &mut in struct fields,
35. // so we declare it as an external type.
36. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
37. #[verifier::external_type_specification]
38. #[verifier::external_body]
39. pub struct ExCacheGuard<'a, V>(crate::CacheGuard<'a, V>);
40. 
41. //==================================================================================================
42. // CacheView - Abstract Specification Model
43. //==================================================================================================
44. 
45. /// Abstract view of a bounded LRU cache.
46. ///
47. /// - `contents`: the key-value mapping of all cached entries.
48. /// - `capacity`: maximum number of entries.
49. /// - `lru_order`: keys ordered from LRU (index 0) to MRU (last element).
50. #[verifier::ext_equal]
51. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(K)]
52. #[verifier::reject_recursive_types(V)]
53. pub struct CacheView<K, V> {
54.     pub contents: Map<K, V>,
55.     pub capacity: nat,
56.     pub lru_order: Seq<K>,
57. }
58. 
59. impl<K, V> CacheView<K, V> {
60. 
61.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
62.     // Well-formedness Invariant
63.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
64. 
65.     /// Well-formedness invariant for the abstract cache state.
66.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
67.         // Size never exceeds capacity.
68.         &&& self.contents.dom().len() <= self.capacity
69.         // LRU order has no duplicates.
70.         &&& self.lru_order.no_duplicates()
71.         // LRU order contains exactly the stored keys.
72.         &&& self.lru_order.to_set() == self.contents.dom()
73.         // Explicit cardinality link (helps the solver).
74.         &&& self.lru_order.len() == self.contents.dom().len()
75.     }
76. 
77.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
78.     // Helper Spec Functions
79.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
80. 
81.     /// Move `key` to the most-recently-used position (end of the sequence).
82.     /// Preserves all other elements and their relative order.
83.     pub open spec fn move_to_mru(self, key: K) -> Seq<K> {
84.         self.lru_order.filter(|k: K| k != key).push(key)
85.     }
86. 
87.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
88.     // Spec Transition Functions
89.     //----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
90. 
91.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::new`.
92.     pub open spec fn spec_new(capacity: nat) -> CacheView<K, V> {
93.         CacheView {
94.             contents: Map::empty(),
95.             capacity,
96.             lru_order: Seq::empty(),
97.         }
98.     }
99. 
100.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::get`.
101.     /// Returns the updated cache state and the lookup result.
102.     pub open spec fn spec_get(self, key: K) -> (CacheView<K, V>, Option<V>) {
103.         if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
104.             (CacheView {
105.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
106.                 ..self
107.             }, Some(self.contents[key]))
108.         } else {
109.             (self, None)
110.         }
111.     }
112. 
113.     /// Spec transition for `Cache::put`.
114.     pub open spec fn spec_put(self, key: K, value: V) -> CacheView<K, V> {
115.         if self.capacity == 0 {
116.             // Zero-capacity cache: no-op.
117.             self
118.         } else if self.contents.dom().contains(key) {
119.             // Overwrite existing key: replace value, refresh recency.
120.             CacheView {
121.                 contents: self.contents.insert(key, value),
122.                 lru_order: self.move_to_mru(key),
123.                 ..self
124.             }
125.         } else if self.contents.dom().len() >= self.capacity {
126.             // At capacity with new key: evict LRU victim, then insert.
127.             let victim = self.lru_order[0];
128.             CacheView {
129.                 contents: self.contents.remove(victim).insert(key, value),

1. # Trust Boundary Audit — libs/cache
2. 
3. This file documents all trust items (external_body, admit, external_type_specification)
4. used in the cache crate verification.
5. 
6. ## Root Cause
7. 
8. vstd provides BTreeMap specifications in `vstd::std_specs::btree` (View trait,
9. `assume_specification` for `new`, `insert`, `get`, `remove`, `clear`, `len`, `iter`,
10. `contains_key`, `keys`, `values`). However, the btree module is gated behind
11. `cfg(all(feature = "alloc", feature = "std"))` and internally imports from
12. `std::collections`, making it structurally incompatible with this crate's `no_std`
13. kernel target (`-Z build-std=core,alloc,compiler_builtins`). Enabling the `std`
14. feature is not possible because the `std` crate does not exist on the i686-nanvix
15. kernel target.
16. 
17. Additionally, `BTreeMap::get_mut` (used by `Cache::get` and `Cache::put`) has no
18. vstd spec even in the `std` btree module, and returns `Option<&mut V>` — a Verus
19. limitation on `&mut` return types.
20. 
21. `CacheGuard` contains `&'a mut V` which Verus cannot handle in struct
22. fields ("The verifier does not yet support &mut types, except in special cases").
23. 
24. ## External Type Specifications
25. 
26. ### ExBTreeMap — `lib.spec.rs:20-23`
27. - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification` + `external_body`
28. - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
29. - **Reason:** `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` is not in vstd. Verus requires a type
30.   declaration to reference it in verified structs. `external_body` is needed because
31.   BTreeMap has private fields.
32. - **Reproducer:** Any `#[verus_verify]` struct containing `BTreeMap<K, V>` fails with
33.   "cannot use type `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` which is ignored because it is either
34.   declared outside the verus! macro or it is marked as `external`."
35. 
36. ### ExGlobal — `lib.spec.rs:25-26`
37. - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification`
38. - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
39. - **Reason:** `alloc::alloc::Global` is the default allocator for `BTreeMap<K, V>`.
40.   Declaring BTreeMap requires this type to be visible to Verus.
41. 
42. ### ExCacheEntry — `lib.spec.rs:29-31`
43. - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification`
44. - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
45. - **Reason:** `CacheEntry<V>` is a private struct used as the value type in
46.   `BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>`. Verus needs to see it to verify Cache.
47. 
48. ### ExCacheGuard — `lib.spec.rs:35-38`
49. - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification` + `external_body`
50. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
51. - **Reason:** `CacheGuard<'a, V>` has field `value: &'a mut V`. Verus does not
52.   support `&mut` in struct field types. `external_body` hides the struct fields.
53. - **Reproducer:** Adding `#[verus_verify]` to `CacheGuard` produces
54.   "The verifier does not yet support &mut types, except in special cases".
55. 
56. ## external_body Functions
57. 
58. ### Cache::new — `lib.rs:147`
59. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
60. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
61. - **Reason:** Body calls `BTreeMap::new()`. vstd btree specs unavailable on
62.   `no_std` target (see Root Cause). Cache::view() is uninterp, so body cannot
63.   be verified against abstract state even with specs.
64. - **Spec:** `result@ == CacheView::spec_new(capacity as nat)`
65. 
66. ### Cache::get — `lib.rs:186`
67. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
68. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
69. - **Reason:** Body calls `BTreeMap::get_mut()` which (a) has no vstd spec even
70.   in the `std` btree module, and (b) returns `Option<&mut V>` — a Verus `&mut`
71.   return type limitation. Also constructs `CacheGuard` with `&mut`.
72. - **Spec:** On hit: `result is Some`, guard view equals `spec_get(*key).1.unwrap()`,
73.   state transitions via `spec_get`. On miss: `result is None`, view unchanged.
74. 
75. ### CacheGuard::deref — `lib.rs:95`
76. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
77. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
78. - **Reason:** CacheGuard is `external_body` (Verus cannot see `&mut V` field).
79.   The body `self.value` accesses the opaque field.
80. - **Spec:** `*ret == self@` — dereferencing yields the guard's abstract value.
81. 
82. ### Cache::put — `lib.rs:216`
83. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
84. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
85. - **Reason:** Same `get_mut` blockers as Cache::get (no vstd spec, `&mut` return
86.   type), plus calls `self.evict()`. vstd btree specs unavailable on `no_std` target.
87. - **Spec:** `self@ == old(self)@.spec_put(key, value)`, invariant preserved.
88. 
89. ### Cache::remove — `lib.rs:262`
90. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
91. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
92. - **Reason:** Calls `BTreeMap::remove()`. vstd btree specs unavailable on
93.   `no_std` target (see Root Cause).
94. - **Spec:** `self@ == old(self)@.spec_remove(*key)`, invariant preserved.
95. 
96. ### Cache::clear — `lib.rs:279`
97. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
98. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
99. - **Reason:** Calls `BTreeMap::clear()`. vstd btree specs unavailable on
100.   `no_std` target (see Root Cause).
101. - **Spec:** `self@ == old(self)@.spec_clear()`, invariant preserved.
102. 
103. ### Cache::evict — `lib.rs:303`
104. - **Trust item:** `external_body`
105. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
106. - **Reason:** Uses `self.entries.iter().min_by_key(|(_, e)| e.last_used)`
107.   iterator chain with closure, plus `BTreeMap::remove()`. Iterator combinators
108.   lack vstd specs. vstd btree specs unavailable on `no_std` target.
109. - **Spec:** LRU victim (`lru_order[0]`) evicted, contents/order updated accordingly.
110. 
111. ## Unverifiable Functions
112. 
113. ### CacheGuard::deref_mut — `lib.rs:101`
114. - **Trust item:** No spec (function excluded from verification)
115. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
116. - **Reason:** `deref_mut` returns `&mut V`. Verus error: "The verifier does not
117.   yet support &mut types, except in special cases" (on the function signature).
118.   The function cannot have any spec annotation at all.
119. - **Reproducer:** Adding `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` to `deref_mut` produces
120.   the `&mut` type error.
121. - **Impact:** Mutation-through-guard semantics are unmodeled. Callers who mutate
122.   a value through `*guard = new_value` have no formal guarantee the change
123.   persists in the cache. This is documented but cannot be resolved until Verus
124.   adds `&mut` return type support.
125. 
126. ## Trust Assumptions
127. 
128. ### Counter overflow — `lib.rs:192,224`
129. - **Assumption:** `self.counter` (type `u64`) never overflows during the
130.   lifetime of a Cache instance.
131. - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION` (precondition omitted)
132. - **Justification:** At 10 billion ops/sec, overflow requires ~58 years.

 # Trust Boundary Audit — libs/cache
 
 This file documents all trust items (external_body, admit, external_type_specification)
 used in the cache crate verification.
 
 ## Root Cause
 
 vstd provides BTreeMap specifications in `vstd::std_specs::btree` (View trait,
 `assume_specification` for `new`, `insert`, `get`, `remove`, `clear`, `len`, `iter`,
 `contains_key`, `keys`, `values`). However, the btree module is gated behind
 `cfg(all(feature = "alloc", feature = "std"))` and internally imports from
 `std::collections`, making it structurally incompatible with this crate's `no_std`
 kernel target (`-Z build-std=core,alloc,compiler_builtins`). Enabling the `std`
 feature is not possible because the `std` crate does not exist on the i686-nanvix
 kernel target.
 
 Additionally, `BTreeMap::get_mut` (used by `Cache::get` and `Cache::put`) has no
 vstd spec even in the `std` btree module, and returns `Option<&mut V>` — a Verus
 limitation on `&mut` return types.
 
 `CacheGuard` contains `&'a mut V` which Verus cannot handle in struct
 fields ("The verifier does not yet support &mut types, except in special cases").
 
 ## External Type Specifications
 
 ### ExBTreeMap — `lib.spec.rs:20-23`
 - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification` + `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
 - **Reason:** `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` is not in vstd. Verus requires a type
   declaration to reference it in verified structs. `external_body` is needed because
   BTreeMap has private fields.
 - **Reproducer:** Any `#[verus_verify]` struct containing `BTreeMap<K, V>` fails with
   "cannot use type `alloc::collections::BTreeMap` which is ignored because it is either
   declared outside the verus! macro or it is marked as `external`."
 
 ### ExGlobal — `lib.spec.rs:25-26`
 - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification`
 - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
 - **Reason:** `alloc::alloc::Global` is the default allocator for `BTreeMap<K, V>`.
   Declaring BTreeMap requires this type to be visible to Verus.
 
 ### ExCacheEntry — `lib.spec.rs:29-31`
 - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification`
 - **Classification:** `EXTERNAL_TYPE`
 - **Reason:** `CacheEntry<V>` is a private struct used as the value type in
   `BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>`. Verus needs to see it to verify Cache.
 
 ### ExCacheGuard — `lib.spec.rs:35-38`
 - **Trust item:** `external_type_specification` + `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** `CacheGuard<'a, V>` has field `value: &'a mut V`. Verus does not
   support `&mut` in struct field types. `external_body` hides the struct fields.
 - **Reproducer:** Adding `#[verus_verify]` to `CacheGuard` produces
   "The verifier does not yet support &mut types, except in special cases".
 
 ## external_body Functions
 
 ### Cache::new — `lib.rs:147`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** Body calls `BTreeMap::new()`. vstd btree specs unavailable on
   `no_std` target (see Root Cause). Cache::view() is uninterp, so body cannot
   be verified against abstract state even with specs.
 - **Spec:** `result@ == CacheView::spec_new(capacity as nat)`
 
 ### Cache::get — `lib.rs:186`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** Body calls `BTreeMap::get_mut()` which (a) has no vstd spec even
   in the `std` btree module, and (b) returns `Option<&mut V>` — a Verus `&mut`
   return type limitation. Also constructs `CacheGuard` with `&mut`.
 - **Spec:** On hit: `result is Some`, guard view equals `spec_get(*key).1.unwrap()`,
   state transitions via `spec_get`. On miss: `result is None`, view unchanged.
 
 ### CacheGuard::deref — `lib.rs:95`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** CacheGuard is `external_body` (Verus cannot see `&mut V` field).
   The body `self.value` accesses the opaque field.
 - **Spec:** `*ret == self@` — dereferencing yields the guard's abstract value.
 
 ### Cache::put — `lib.rs:216`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** Same `get_mut` blockers as Cache::get (no vstd spec, `&mut` return
   type), plus calls `self.evict()`. vstd btree specs unavailable on `no_std` target.
 - **Spec:** `self@ == old(self)@.spec_put(key, value)`, invariant preserved.
 
 ### Cache::remove — `lib.rs:262`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** Calls `BTreeMap::remove()`. vstd btree specs unavailable on
   `no_std` target (see Root Cause).
 - **Spec:** `self@ == old(self)@.spec_remove(*key)`, invariant preserved.
 
 ### Cache::clear — `lib.rs:279`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** Calls `BTreeMap::clear()`. vstd btree specs unavailable on
   `no_std` target (see Root Cause).
 - **Spec:** `self@ == old(self)@.spec_clear()`, invariant preserved.
 
 ### Cache::evict — `lib.rs:303`
 - **Trust item:** `external_body`
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** Uses `self.entries.iter().min_by_key(|(_, e)| e.last_used)`
   iterator chain with closure, plus `BTreeMap::remove()`. Iterator combinators
   lack vstd specs. vstd btree specs unavailable on `no_std` target.
 - **Spec:** LRU victim (`lru_order[0]`) evicted, contents/order updated accordingly.
 
 ## Unverifiable Functions
 
 ### CacheGuard::deref_mut — `lib.rs:101`
 - **Trust item:** No spec (function excluded from verification)
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION`
 - **Reason:** `deref_mut` returns `&mut V`. Verus error: "The verifier does not
   yet support &mut types, except in special cases" (on the function signature).
   The function cannot have any spec annotation at all.
 - **Reproducer:** Adding `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` to `deref_mut` produces
   the `&mut` type error.
 - **Impact:** Mutation-through-guard semantics are unmodeled. Callers who mutate
   a value through `*guard = new_value` have no formal guarantee the change
   persists in the cache. This is documented but cannot be resolved until Verus
   adds `&mut` return type support.
 
 ## Trust Assumptions
 
 ### Counter overflow — `lib.rs:192,224`
 - **Assumption:** `self.counter` (type `u64`) never overflows during the
   lifetime of a Cache instance.
 - **Classification:** `VERUS_LIMITATION` (precondition omitted)
 - **Justification:** At 10 billion ops/sec, overflow requires ~58 years.
   Physically unreachable. Adding `requires self.counter < u64::MAX` would
   burden every caller with a practically-impossible proof obligation.
 - **See also:** `bugs.md` BUG-1.
 
 ## admit() in Proof Stubs
 
 All five admit() placeholders have been eliminated. The invariant preservation
 lemmas are now fully proven:
 
 | Lemma | Status |
 |---|---|
 | `lemma_spec_new_inv` | ✅ Proven |
 | `lemma_spec_get_inv` | ✅ Proven |
 | `lemma_spec_put_inv` | ✅ Proven |
 | `lemma_spec_remove_inv` | ✅ Proven |
 | `lemma_spec_clear_inv` | ✅ Proven |

2. 
3. ## BUG-1: Counter overflow (u64)
4. 
5. - **Status:** UNCONFIRMED
6. - **Severity:** LOW (physically unreachable)
7. - **Location:** `lib.rs` — `Cache::get` (line ~192) and `Cache::put` (line ~224)
8. - **Description:** The `counter: u64` field is incremented on every `get` hit and
9.   `put` call without overflow checking (`self.counter += 1`). After 2^64
10.   operations the counter wraps to 0, which would corrupt LRU ordering —
11.   freshly accessed entries would have a lower counter than old ones, causing
12.   incorrect eviction.
13. - **Impact:** At 10 billion ops/sec, overflow requires ~58 years of continuous
14.   operation. Physically unreachable in practice, but the spec does not model
15.   this assumption.
16. - **Spec gap:** No `requires self.counter < u64::MAX` precondition exists.
17.   The spec transition functions use abstract `Seq` ordering (not counters),
18.   so the spec is correct even if the implementation overflows — but the
19.   `external_body` trust gap means the implementation's correctness depends
20.   on no overflow occurring.
21. - **Recommendation:** Document as a trust assumption. Optionally add
22.   `debug_assert!(self.counter < u64::MAX)` or use `checked_add`.
23.

3. 
4. //! Bounded LRU cache backed by `BTreeMap`.
5. //!
6. //! Entries are stored in a `BTreeMap` keyed by a caller-chosen type `K` that
7. //! implements `Ord + Clone`. A monotonic counter tracks access order; on
8. //! eviction the entry with the smallest (oldest) counter value is removed.
9. //! Lookups bump the counter to mark the entry as recently used.
10. //!
11. //! # Capacity
12. //!
13. //! The cache is bounded by a capacity given at construction time. When the
14. //! cache is full, the least-recently-used entry is evicted before inserting a
15. //! new one.
16. //!
17. //! # Example
18. //!
19. //! ```
20. //! use cache::Cache;
21. //!
22. //! let mut cache: Cache<&str, i32> = Cache::new(2);
23. //! cache.put("a", 1);
24. //! cache.put("b", 2);
25. //! assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"a").unwrap(), 1);
26. //!
27. //! // Inserting a third entry evicts "b" (least recently used).
28. //! cache.put("c", 3);
29. //! assert!(cache.get(&"b").is_none());
30. //! assert_eq!(*cache.get(&"c").unwrap(), 3);
31. //! ```
32. 
33. #![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]
34. #![cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, feature(proc_macro_hygiene))]
35. #![cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, feature(allocator_api))]
36. 
37. //==================================================================================================
38. // Imports
39. //==================================================================================================
40. 
41. extern crate alloc;
42. 
43. use ::alloc::collections::BTreeMap;
44. use ::core::ops::{
45.     Deref,
46.     DerefMut,
47. };
48. 
49. use vstd::prelude::*;
50. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
51. include!("lib.spec.rs");
52. #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
53. include!("lib.proof.rs");
54. 
55. 
56. //==================================================================================================
57. // Cache Entry
58. //==================================================================================================
59. 
60. /// A single entry in the cache.
61. #[derive(Clone)]
62. struct CacheEntry<V> {
63.     /// Cached value.
64.     value: V,
65.     /// Last-access counter (higher = more recently used).
66.     last_used: u64,
67. }
68. 
69. //==================================================================================================
70. // Cache Guard
71. //==================================================================================================
72. 
73. ///
74. /// # Description
75. ///
76. /// RAII guard providing a reference to a cached entry.
77. ///
78. /// Created by [`Cache::get()`]. Dereferences to `&V` for read access
79. /// and `&mut V` for write access. The LRU counter is bumped when the guard
80. /// is created.
81. ///
82. pub struct CacheGuard<'a, V> {
83.     /// Mutable reference to the cached value.
84.     value: &'a mut V,
85. }
86. 
87. #[verus_verify]
88. impl<V> Deref for CacheGuard<'_, V> {
89.     type Target = V;
90. 
91.     #[verus_verify(external_body)]
92.     #[verus_spec(ret =>
93.         ensures *ret == self@,
94.     )]
95.     fn deref(&self) -> &V {
96.         self.value
97.     }
98. }
99. 
100. impl<V> DerefMut for CacheGuard<'_, V> {
101.     fn deref_mut(&mut self) -> &mut V {
102.         self.value
103.     }
104. }
105. 
106. //==================================================================================================
107. // Cache
108. //==================================================================================================
109. 
110. ///
111. /// # Description
112. ///
113. /// A bounded cache using access-counter LRU approximation.
114. ///
115. /// Entries are stored in a `BTreeMap` keyed by `K`. A monotonic counter tracks access order;
116. /// on eviction the entry with the smallest (oldest) counter value is removed. Lookups bump the
117. /// counter to mark the entry as recently used.
118. ///
119. #[verus_verify(reject_recursive_types(K))]
120. #[verus_verify(reject_recursive_types(V))]
121. pub struct Cache<K, V> {
122.     /// Cached entries.
123.     entries: BTreeMap<K, CacheEntry<V>>,
124.     /// Monotonically increasing counter for LRU ordering.
125.     counter: u64,
126.     /// Maximum number of entries.
127.     capacity: usize,
128. }
129. 
130. #[verus_verify]
131. impl<K: Ord + Clone, V> Cache<K, V> {
132.     ///
133.     /// # Description
134.     ///
135.     /// Creates a new empty cache with the given capacity.
136.     ///
137.     /// # Parameters
138.     ///
